items.subtopic: Domain structure and the CISO mandate
items.title: CISM Domain Structure and the CISO's Mandate
items.summary: How the CISM domains fit together, what each one actually asks of a security leader, and what the CISO is genuinely accountable for when the board asks them to certify the organisation's risk position.
objectives: Describe the four CISM domains and the published weighting of each domain
Explain the CISO mandate in terms of decision rights, advice and assurance rather than tools
Distinguish governance, risk management, programme development and operations management
Position your current role against the domain structure and identify the gap to close

sections.heading: What CISM Actually Certifies
sections.body:
CISM is a management certification, not a technical one. ISACA's framing is consistent across the certification family: the exam tests whether you can govern, direct and control information security as a business function. A candidate who can configure a firewall perfectly but cannot get a business unit to fund a control has not demonstrated the competence the certification is designed to attest.

The practical consequence is that the syllabus is organised around the lifecycle of an information security function inside a business: why it exists, how it is governed, how risk is identified and treated, how the programme is built and funded, and how it operates day to day. Every domain maps onto a set of decisions that a security leader either makes, influences, or escalates. If you cannot name the decision attached to a topic, you have not yet learned the topic in the sense the exam and the job require.

A second consequence, and one that surprises candidates coming from a technical background, is that the domain structure is deliberately manager-shaped. The domains cover strategy, risk, programme, operations, incident response, continuity and business alignment. They do not cover the mechanics of exploit development, reverse engineering or tool configuration. You can be an excellent security engineer and a poor CISM candidate, and equally you can be a mediocre engineer and an excellent CISO, because the two roles answer to different questions.
bullets: CISM tests governance judgement: can you make and defend decisions about information security in a business context
Technical depth is assumed to be delegated to specialists; the exam asks whether you direct them well
Domain boundaries matter because real jobs do not respect them - you will be assessed on reasoning across domains
The certification is vendor-neutral and sits alongside CISA, CRISC and CGEIT in ISACA's family

sections.heading: The Four Domains and Their Published Weightings
sections.body:
The published CISM exam outline divides the body of knowledge into four domains. In the outline ISACA published for the current version of the exam, the weightings were Information Security Governance at 25 per cent, Information Risk Management at 20 per cent, Information Security Program Development and Management at 25 per cent, and Information Security Operations Management at 20 per cent. Treat those numbers as indicative of emphasis rather than as fixed truth: ISACA revises the outline periodically, and you should check the current candidate handbook before you plan study time.

What the numbers actually tell you is where the exam believes the marginal difficulty sits. Governance and programme development carry the heaviest weight because both are about making many people do things consistently over years without authority over most of them. Risk management is weighted for the judgement calls around assessment, treatment and acceptance. Operations carries a lower weight not because it is unimportant but because it is the domain where candidate experience most often substitutes for study.

This module teaches the four domains in the order they appear in the syllabus, with Domain 1 spread across three lessons, Domain 2 across two, Domain 3 across three and Domain 4 across three. Where a domain's practice has been reshaped by regulation - for example the way Indian CERT-In directions and RBI expectations have hardened security governance requirements since 2018 - we cover both the certification framing and the working reality.
table: Who decides, under what authority, and how is the decision evidenced?
What could go wrong, how much does it matter, and what do we do about it?
Information Security Program Development and Management
How do we build, fund, resource and improve the programme?
How do we run the programme day to day, including incidents and continuity?
sections.callout: Check the current ISACA exam outline and candidate handbook before you commit a study plan. Syllabi and weightings are revised, and this module is written to the structure as published at the time of writing rather than to a frozen document.

sections.heading: The CISO Mandate: From Technical Authority to Enterprise Advisor
sections.body:
The single most useful reframe for a new security leader is that the CISO owns a decision right, not a tool estate. A CISO who cannot make a decision that changes how the business spends money, accepts risk, or ships a product has not secured the mandate, regardless of how good the technical estate looks. Mandate has four components that you should be able to articulate for any organisation.

First, authority: a defined scope covering the assets, systems and data the organisation relies on, and a documented right to be consulted on changes that affect them. Second, position: a reporting line that preserves objectivity. A CISO reporting into the head of the business unit whose risks they assess cannot set risk appetite for that unit. Third, resources: a budget, a headcount and a mandate to allocate both across the portfolio rather than reactively. Fourth, standing: the right to raise an issue to the board without routing it through the person whose budget it affects.

Notice what is not in that list. It is not the CISO's job to make every risk acceptable, and it is not the CISO's job to prevent every incident. The professional position is that the CISO provides the information and options for informed risk decisions by accountable business owners, and is accountable for the security of the environment in which those decisions are taken. When an incident occurs, the question that matters is whether the decision was informed and whether the treatment matched the recorded appetite. That is the standard of professional practice, and it is what you will be assessed against in Domain 4.
bullets: Authority: written scope of the systems, data and locations you cover
Position: reporting line that keeps you independent of the risk owners
Resources: a budget and the ability to allocate it across the portfolio
Standing: direct, unfiltered access to the board risk committee
Accountability: for the security environment and the advice, not for outcomes the business controls

sections.heading: How the Domains Interlock
sections.body:
Most real work crosses domain boundaries, which is why the exam asks for judgement rather than recall and why real job interviews probe how you handle the seams. A single worked example will show you the seams better than any diagram.

A bank launches a mobile lending product in six months. Domain 1 is engaged first: what is the security strategy for digital origination, which committee approves the risk acceptance if fraud losses exceed appetite, and does the existing policy framework even cover third-party origination risk. Domain 2 then assesses the risk: what is the fraud exposure, what is the impact of a data breach on the lending book, and what control set brings residual risk within tolerance. Domain 3 builds the programme: does the current team have the capacity, what does the tooling cost, who supplies the continuous monitoring. Domain 4 runs it: who watches the dashboards, who is on call, what happens when the mobile app has a critical defect in production, and how the incident feeds the next strategy revision.

Notice the loop at the end. Domain 4's operational data - fraud rates, false positive rates, incident volumes, control exceptions - is the raw material for Domain 1's next strategy cycle. Mature security functions make that loop explicit by reporting the same metrics at the board risk committee that the operations team sees every morning. Weak functions run a governance cycle annually that bears no relationship to what happened last Tuesday.
bullets: Governance sets the direction and the decision rights
Risk management translates direction into quantified, owned risk positions
Programme management turns treatment plans into funded, staffed, evidenced work
Operations management produces the evidence that the other three domains need
The cycle repeats: operational data must flow back into strategy, or the strategy is fiction

sections.heading: Common Misunderstandings
sections.body:
Four misconceptions account for most of the avoidable failures in CISM candidates and newly promoted CISOs. The first is that governance means writing policy. It does not. A policy nobody has operationalised and cannot be evidenced is a liability, because it creates a documented obligation with no control behind it, and an auditor will find it.

The second is that risk management is a scoring exercise. Risk work is communication and decision support. If the register does not lead to a decision by an accountable owner, it is administration.

The third is that programme development is project delivery. Delivering a project on time and inside budget says nothing about whether the capability is repeatable, evidenced, or adequately staffed for the next year.

The fourth is that operations means keeping the lights on. Operations is where the organisation finds out whether the design was right. A security function that has never had to respond to a real incident at three in the morning has a theory, not a capability.
sections.callout: If you can only remember one thing from this lesson: the CISO's job is to make security decisions well, document them, and keep the evidence. Everything else in the syllabus is a way of doing that.

examples.title: A newly appointed CISO inheriting a loosely defined mandate
examples.context: You join a mid-sized retail bank with 1,800 employees as its first CISO. There is a security operations team of nine reporting to the Head of IT. Policies exist but were last reviewed four years ago. Your position in the org chart is Head of IT Security, which means your manager also owns the infrastructure budget and the uptime targets you are measured against. The board has never received a security report.
examples.outcome: A good outcome is a documented mandate covering scope, decisions, resources and board access, agreed with the CEO and the board chair, with an independence mechanism that lets you raise issues about IT-owned systems. The first deliverable is not a tool; it is a one-page mandate statement approved at board level, plus an agreement on how and when the board will hear from you.

examples.title: From solo operator to enterprise function in manufacturing
examples.context: Your organisation makes industrial equipment in three plants and sells to hospitals. You were hired as IT manager and you now also cover security because the company cannot afford a CISO. IT, OT and a new e-commerce channel all depend on you. Leadership wants a single vendor to quote an all-in security service and wants you to sign off on it.
examples.outcome: A good outcome is that you do not accept a single-vendor answer by default. You build a risk-scoped view first: which plants have safety implications, which contracts require security commitments from you, which suppliers already hold security obligations, and what the customer base implies. You then evaluate vendors against that scope and documented requirements, and you tell leadership explicitly which risks you are accepting under a fixed budget. You also make the case, in writing, for the minimum separation of duties the role requires.

practicalExercise.title: Map your organisation against the four CISM domains
practicalExercise.brief: You will produce a one-page gap assessment of an organisation you know well - yours, or one described below - against each of the four CISM domains, ending with a ranked list of the three gaps you would raise with the executive team first.
steps: Write a two-sentence description of the organisation: its sector, size, business model, and the two or three assets whose loss or compromise would most damage the business.

For each of the four CISM domains, list what already exists (documents, committees, systems, named roles) and what the domain would require but you cannot evidence. Be concrete: a policy name, a meeting, a report, a person.
For Domain 1 only, write a draft mandate statement for the security leader covering scope, decision rights, resources and board access, and mark which of the four elements is currently absent.
Mark each gap as blocked by mandate, blocked by money, blocked by people or blocked by will. This distinction changes who you need to persuade.

Rank all gaps against a single criterion - exposure to loss of the critical assets you named in step one - and select your top three. Write one sentence per gap explaining the consequence of leaving it open for the next twelve months.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A one-page gap map with the four domains as headings, an evidence list and a gap list under each, plus a ranked top-three list with consequence statements.
evaluationCriteria: Every gap cites concrete evidence - a named document, meeting, system or role - rather than describing an abstraction
The mandate statement is complete on scope, decision rights, resources and board access, and honestly identifies what is missing
Gaps are distinguished by their blocker, and the argument for each top-three item is tied to loss of the identified critical assets
The document is readable by an executive who has no security background, with no unexplained jargon

items.title: CISM Domain 1 - Information Security Governance
items.summary: How to build a security strategy that survives board scrutiny, design a tiered and testable policy architecture, and run governance committees that make and record real decisions.
objectives: Distinguish governance, management and operations and apply that distinction to security
Design a security strategy that ties to business objectives and carries a costed roadmap
Construct a tiered policy architecture with version control, owners and review triggers
Run a governance committee that produces documented decisions with named owners and dates

sections.heading: Governance Is a Decision Right, Not a Document
sections.body:
The most expensive mistake in information security governance is the belief that producing a policy creates governance. It does not. A policy is a record of a decision that someone with authority already made. Governance is the machinery that produces those decisions and holds people to them. If your organisation has forty policy documents and a security steering committee that has met twice in three years, you have documentation without governance.

Governance in the security context has three working parts. The first is the decision framework: who is authorised to accept risk, approve exceptions, sign off on major changes, and set tolerance. The second is the assurance mechanism: how the executive team and the board learn that the decisions are being made and honoured, including the ones that go against the recommendation of the security function. The third is escalation: what happens when a business owner will not accept the treatment you advise, or a regulator, auditor or customer asks a question you cannot answer.

Test your governance with a simple test. Ask a business owner to describe, in their own words, the level of disruption their team would accept for a planned change to a customer-facing system. If the answer is vague, you do not have governance - you have a policy that nobody internalised. Governance that works shows up in behaviour before it shows up in documentation.
bullets: Governance decides; management executes; operations delivers day to day
The test of a governance mechanism is whether a real decision was made, recorded and honoured
Escalation paths are part of governance, not an afterthought - define them before the first conflict

sections.heading: Building a Security Strategy That Survives Board Scrutiny
sections.body:
A security strategy is not a technology plan and it is not a list of controls. Its job is to state where the organisation chooses to take risk, where it refuses to, and how it will know whether the choice was sound. The structure that survives a board is simple: business context, objectives, principles, measurable outcomes, and a costed roadmap with dates.

Start with the business context in the business's own language. If you open with a maturity model score, the board stops listening. Open with what the organisation does, which assets are irreplaceable, what would hurt the business most if they were unavailable or disclosed, and which regulators and customers constrain the choices. Then state three to five security objectives phrased as outcomes the board cares about - for example, no unplanned customer-facing outage caused by information security exceeding four hours per quarter, and every material incident reported to the board within twenty-four hours of confirmation.

The roadmap is where most strategies fail credibility. A strategy with no costed roadmap is a wish list, and it will be funded last in a tight budget cycle. Pair each objective with the initiatives that deliver it, a first-year cost, a named accountable executive, and a dependency on the business - because almost every meaningful security control requires the business to change something, whether that is a process, a contract or a behaviour. A roadmap with no business dependency column is usually a security wish list disguised as a plan.
table: Could a non-executive read it and name the business risk?
Vague verbs such as improve or strengthen
Is every objective measurable with a number and a date?
Could a business owner use it to reject an exception?
No cost, no owner, no dependencies
Does every initiative have a cost, an owner and a business dependency?
sections.callout: A board approves a strategy when they can see which decisions it will let them make better. If your strategy only describes what security will do, it is an operating plan and belongs one level down.

sections.heading: The Policy Architecture: Tiered, Versioned and Testable
sections.body:
Most organisations have a policy document problem in both directions at once: too many near-duplicate policies with contradictory requirements, and no policy at all in the areas where the business is actually exposed. The fix is architecture, not volume. A workable structure is three tiers.

Tier one is the information security policy approved by the board - one document, a page or two, setting intent, scope, roles and the commitments the organisation makes. Tier two is the policy set, organised by theme, each owned by a named executive and each containing the requirements that other functions can comply with. Tier three is the standards, procedures and guidelines that say how the requirements are met in practice.

Every policy needs six attributes to be worth the paper it is on: an owner who can be held to it, an approval body, a version and an effective date, a review cadence, a documented exception process, and a statement of what happens when it is breached. That last one is the one most often missing, and it is the one that makes a policy real - consequences named in advance are enforceable; consequences discovered afterwards are negotiable.

Version control is not administrative tidiness. It determines whether you can prove what applied on the day of the incident. Keep superseded versions, keep an approval trail, and record which version was in force on any given date. Review triggers matter more than the calendar: a policy should be reopened when there is a regulatory change, a major incident, a significant business change, an audit finding, or a change in the threat landscape - not merely because three years elapsed.
bullets: Tier 1: board-approved information security policy - intent, scope, roles, commitments
Tier 2: thematic policy set - owned by executives, containing requirements other functions can comply with
Tier 3: standards, procedures and guidelines - how the requirements are met
Mandatory attributes: owner, approver, version, effective date, review cadence, exception route, breach consequence
Review on trigger events as well as on a calendar; keep superseded versions for evidential purposes

sections.heading: Governance Committees: Mandate, Cadence and Paper
sections.body:
A security governance committee is a decision forum. If it only receives updates, it is a status meeting and should be renamed and shortened. The design of the committee determines what the organisation can actually decide, and the three things that determine it are the mandate, the membership and the cadence.

The mandate should list the decisions reserved to the committee: approving or recommending risk acceptance above a defined threshold, approving exceptions to policy, approving material changes to the security architecture, approving the security programme plan and budget, and confirming risk closure. Membership should be the business owners who can make those decisions - not their deputies unless the deputies hold the same authority. A committee of information security staff is a working group wearing a committee's clothes.

Cadence should match the decision frequency. A monthly governance committee for a large regulated organisation, quarterly for a mid-sized one, and monthly for a small one are all defensible. What is not defensible is a quarterly committee receiving monthly data, because the committee then discusses stale exceptions and no longer holds the pulse.

Paper discipline is what separates a committee that governs from one that performs. Every agenda item should have a decision owner, a decision requested, and a recommended position from the security function. Every minute should record the decision, the conditions attached, the accountable owner and a due date, and should list carried-forward items with their age. If the same item has been carried three times, that is not a tracking issue; it is evidence that the committee lacks the authority to resolve it, and the right response is to escalate the mandate rather than to keep deferring.
table: Name the decisions reserved to the committee
A mandate written as topics to discuss rather than decisions to take
One decision per item, with owner and date
Minutes that record discussion but no decision

sections.heading: Where Governance Fails in Practice
sections.body:
Governance failures cluster into recognisable patterns, and recognising them is a large part of the professional value a CISO adds.

The first pattern is the compliance recital: the committee receives assurance reports from every regulatory obligation and spends its time tracking them rather than making decisions about risk. The remedy is a unified obligation register with one owner per obligation and a single severity view, so the committee can compare a PCI obligation with an internal control gap on the same page.

The second is the exception treadmill: business owners routinely request exceptions and the committee approves them as a formality. The remedy is to require a treatment plan, an expiry date and a named compensating control for every exception, and to publish the total number and value of open exceptions as a metric.

The third is the risk-acceptance vacuum: nobody wants to sign. The remedy is to make acceptance a positive, bounded act - accept subject to a named control, accept for a stated period, accept with a defined consequence - rather than a refusal to decide. An unsigned acceptance is not a risk-free position; it is an unowned one.

The fourth is the strategy that is never revisited. The remedy is to schedule a formal strategy review each year against the assumptions it was built on, and to require that the assumptions be written down. If the assumption was that the organisation has one cloud provider and it now has three, the strategy was not wrong when written, but it is wrong now.
sections.callout: Governance maturity is measured by the quality of decisions made under pressure, not by the volume of documentation produced when things are calm.

examples.title: Building the first security governance committee in a listed manufacturer
examples.context: A listed industrial manufacturer has ISO 27001 certification, a security manager, and an audit committee that has never received a technology risk paper. The CFO asks what the new committee will cost in meeting time across eleven directors. The security manager wants to include the plant managers, the CTO, and the head of legal.
examples.outcome: A good outcome is a committee with a one-page mandate, six members who can actually approve exceptions and accept risk, a quarterly cadence with monthly exception reporting delegated to the security manager, and a standard pack of five papers: risk position, exception register, incident and continuity summary, programme delivery and budget, and forward look. Directors get a single consolidated pack rather than twelve regulatory recitals.

examples.title: Policy sprawl in a fast-growing IT services firm
examples.context: Your organisation grew from 40 to 400 people in three years. You inherited 63 policy and procedure documents, several of which contradict each other on retention, remote work and encryption. Nobody knows which version applies. A customer audit has just asked to see your encryption policy and you cannot say for certain what it currently requires.
examples.outcome: A good outcome is a documented three-tier architecture with the contradictions resolved by decision, not by deleting the inconvenient document, and a supersession record that shows what was retired and when. The immediate deliverable is an evidence pack that lets you hand the auditor the current encryption policy with its approval date and owner, plus a plan to retire the duplicates on a defined schedule.

practicalExercise.title: Draft a security strategy and governance mandate for a fictional bank
practicalExercise.brief: You are the incoming CISO of a mid-sized cooperative bank with 60 branches, 300 employees and a legacy core banking platform. The board has asked for a security strategy and a governance structure by the end of the quarter.
steps: Write a one-paragraph business context covering the business model, the three assets whose loss would hurt the bank most, and the three external constraints you can identify (regulatory, customer, contractual).

Draft five security objectives as measurable outcomes. Each must contain a number, a measurement source and a target date, and at least two must be about risk reduction rather than about tool deployment.
Draft a costed twelve-month roadmap with four to six initiatives. For each, state cost band, accountable executive, dependency on a business unit, and the strategy objective it serves.
Write a one-page governance mandate naming the decisions reserved to the security governance committee, its membership by role, its cadence, and the standard reporting pack.

Add a paragraph on your own mandate: scope, decision rights, resources and board access, plus one sentence on how you will handle the situation where a business owner refuses your recommended treatment.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A strategy pack of three to four pages covering business context, objectives, roadmap, governance mandate and your own mandate statement.
evaluationCriteria: Objectives are measurable, dated and include at least two that describe a business risk outcome rather than an activity
Every roadmap initiative has a cost band, a named accountable role and at least one business dependency
The governance mandate lists decisions, not topics, and the membership can actually take those decisions
The strategy contains no technology named as an objective; technology appears only as the means of delivery
The mandate statement is specific enough that a reader could hold you to it

items.title: CISM Domain 1 - Roles, Responsibilities and Security Awareness Programmes
items.summary: How to assign ownership without taking it away from the business, apply the three lines model to security, design segregation of duties that actually survives exceptions, and build an awareness programme judged by behaviour rather than completion rates.
objectives: Build a role and responsibility matrix that places ownership with accountable business owners
Apply the three lines model to information security and explain the independence requirement
Design segregation of duties and access management rules that hold under business pressure
Design and measure a security awareness programme using behavioural outcomes

sections.heading: The Role Stack: Who Owns What
sections.body:
Security accountability fails in a predictable way when organisations try to make the security function responsible for outcomes that other people control. Nobody in the CISO's team can decide whether a bank releases a product with a known fraud exposure, whether a hospital schedules surgery, or whether a telecom operator activates a network element with an unreviewed configuration. Those decisions belong to the accountable business owner, and a governance model that pretends otherwise will either fail the audit or, worse, pass the audit while the risk stays unowned.

The role stack that works in practice has four levels. The board and its risk committee own the risk appetite and confirm that the framework is operating. The executive team owns the risk decisions within that appetite, and each executive is accountable for the risks of their own function. The security function owns the framework, the advice, the monitoring, and the escalation - but not the business decisions. Individual process and system owners own the design and operation of their controls, and are the ones who can say what is realistic in their context.

The critical discipline is that ownership of a risk sits with the person who has the authority to change the exposure. If the risk is created by a business process, the business owns it. If the risk is created by an inability to control a technical mechanism, the security function owns the mechanism and advises on the process. Write this down in a responsibility matrix that names roles, not individuals, and that explicitly states who is accountable for each risk category. Publish it, and revisit it whenever the organisation restructures.
bullets: Board and risk committee: set appetite, confirm the framework is operating
Executive team: make risk decisions within appetite, each accountable for their function's risks
Security function: build the framework, advise, monitor, escalate - not the business decision
Control and process owners: design and operate their own controls in their own context
Rule of thumb: the party with authority to change the exposure owns the risk

sections.heading: Three Lines Applied to Information Security
sections.body:
The three lines model, published by the IIA, separates roles that are often muddled in organisations: the first line owns and manages the risk, the second line oversees risk and compliance across the organisation, and the third line provides independent assurance. Applied to security, it produces an important clarification that many organisations have never articulated.

Business process and system owners sit in the first line. They operate the controls, manage the risk in their process, and are accountable for the effectiveness of the controls they run. The security function sits in the second line - with an important caveat that is the subject of the next section - providing framework, policy, independent monitoring, testing and escalation. Internal audit sits in the third line and is independent of everything else, reporting to the audit committee rather than to the CISO.

The caveat matters because many organisations place the security function in the first line by accident: the security operations team configures the firewalls, runs the backups, patches the servers and administers the identity platform. That is first-line work. Doing it while also claiming to provide independent assurance over the same environment is a structural contradiction, and an experienced auditor will find it. The practical resolution depends on scale. In a large organisation, separate the operation of controls from the oversight of them: a team that deploys identity controls should not be the team that reports on identity control effectiveness. In a small organisation, you may not be able to split the roles, and you should say so explicitly rather than pretending the separation exists.
table: Operating firewalls, running the SIEM log pipeline, administering identities, patching
Owners stop feeling accountable for their own risk
Framework, policy, independent testing, risk register, metrics, escalation
Oversight becomes self-review and loses credibility
Assurance is not independent and cannot be relied upon

sections.heading: Segregation of Duties and the Access Request Problem
sections.body:
Segregation of duties is the oldest and most frequently violated control in information security, because the pressure it creates is always commercial and immediate, while the harm it prevents is hypothetical and future. A ticket to add a contractor to the payment release system is delayed by three days, the vendor complains, and someone senior tells the security team to make an exception. Three months later the exception has become the default and the control has effectively been retired.

A workable design separates three things: the request, the approval, and the technical execution. In a healthy model the business owner approves access based on a documented role, security or an automated rule executes it against the role, and a separate periodic review confirms that entitlements still match the role. Where the organisation is too small to separate roles entirely, compensating controls are used, and they must be named: for example, a second-person authorisation on a payment release, with the authorisation and the execution both logged and reviewed monthly.

The access request process itself is where the governance actually lives. What matters is not the ticket system but the decision rules: what constitutes a valid business justification, who may approve which entitlements, what standard evidence is required, how long an approval remains valid, and what happens to entitlements when the role changes. Define a small set of entitlements that carry elevated risk - privileged access, financial transaction capability, bulk data export, production change approval, audit log amendment - and route each through a named authority. Publish the count and age of open privileged access requests as a metric, because a growing queue is a leading indicator of informal workarounds.
bullets: Separate request, approval and execution; where impossible, name the compensating control
Define elevated-entitlement categories and a named approver authority for each
Set approval validity: entitlements expire when the role changes, not when the system does
Monitor privileged access request age and volume as an informal-workaround indicator
Log both approval and execution for compensating controls, and review them on a fixed cadence

sections.heading: Security Awareness as a Measured Programme
sections.body:
Most awareness programmes measure completion, and completion is close to worthless as a risk indicator. A phishing simulation with a 30 per cent click rate and 100 per cent course completion tells you that the training is being consumed and the behaviour is unchanged. If the programme is going to be funded and defended, it must be measured in behaviour, and behaviour has to be tied to specific, few, high-cost actions.

Start by identifying the specific actions that cause the most harm in your organisation. For a bank, that is credential entry into a lookalike domain, payment-detail changes requested by email, and USB insertion. For a hospital, it is sharing credentials at a workstation and clicking unexpected attachments containing patient data. For a telecom operator, it is credential reuse on network management interfaces and disabling of logging for troubleshooting convenience. Awareness content that does not name the organisation's specific dangerous actions is generic and mostly forgotten.

Design for segmented audiences. The general workforce needs short, repeated, scenario-based content matched to the few actions that matter for them. Staff in higher-risk roles - developers, help desk, finance, privileged administrators - need additional, role-specific content and target-specific simulation. Managers need a different message entirely: how to spot a compromised report from their own team, and what to do in the first ten minutes.

Finally, design the measurement. Useful metrics include simulation failure rates by segment, time to report a simulated event, the proportion of privileged users who have completed simulated privilege-escalation tests, and the rate at which reported events are converted into teaching cases. A rising report rate with a falling failure rate is the signature of a programme that is working, because reporting is a behaviour that only grows if people trust that reporting will not be punished.
table: Why it is more useful than completion
Whether the behaviour changed for the targeted audience
Completion can be 100% with unchanged behaviour
Whether people believe reporting is safe and useful
Low reporting usually signals fear of blame
Conversion of reports into teaching cases
Creates the virtuous cycle of visible improvement
Residual risk in the highest-impact population
Privileged compromise is the dominant breach path in many sectors
sections.callout: Design the awareness programme around the organisation's specific dangerous actions, not around the framework's training requirements. The regulatory requirement is the floor, not the design.

examples.title: Segregation of duties under pressure in a payments business
examples.context: Your payments platform processes supplier payouts. The operations team can both add beneficiary accounts and release payments. A new business line needs urgent onboarding and the operations manager asks for a three-month blanket approval to let one analyst handle both, on the grounds that the volume is too high for the current two-person model.
examples.outcome: A good outcome is a decision that reduces the exception rather than granting it: a capacity fix (cross-training, temporary staff, a batch review step) combined with a short, tightly scoped and logged exception covering only the named analyst, only the new business line, only for 30 days, with retrospective review. The quarterly exception report should show the exception ageing, and it should be reported to the governance committee as a business capacity risk, not as a security exception.

examples.title: Awareness measurement in a government health service
examples.context: Your organisation employs 9,000 staff across 12 hospitals and a shared services centre. Mandatory annual training completion is 99 per cent. Internal audit has observed that two of three data breaches over the past year began with a user clicking a link and entering credentials, and the awareness manager has been asked to reduce click rates by 30 per cent.
examples.outcome: A good outcome replaces the completion metric with a behaviour metric and narrows the target population: simulated phishing with scenarios drawn from real local threats, segmented by department, with the three highest-risk departments - emergency, radiology and administration - receiving tailored content on patient-record access. The programme reports simulation failure rate and time-to-report by department to the board risk committee, alongside a case study each quarter showing what was fixed after a report.

practicalExercise.title: Build a role matrix and an awareness measurement plan
practicalExercise.brief: You will produce two artefacts for a fictional organisation: a role and responsibility matrix for information security, and an awareness measurement plan with behavioural metrics.
steps: Choose an organisation (bank, hospital, telco, manufacturer or software firm) and list its six to eight principal risk categories, for example data breach, unauthorised payment, service outage, third-party failure, insider misuse and regulatory breach.

For each risk category, assign a first-line owner, a second-line function and a third-line assurance provider. Write one sentence justifying each assignment, especially where the natural owner and the risk creator differ.
Identify three segregation-of-duties conflicts you can foresee and describe, for each, the compensating control you would require and the metric that would reveal the compensating control failing.
Design an awareness programme for this organisation: name the three specific dangerous actions, define three audience segments and state the message for each.

Write five metrics with their definitions, data sources, collection frequency, target thresholds and the board-level question each metric answers. Replace any completion metric with a behavioural one and note the substitution.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A role and responsibility matrix with justifications, three segregation-of-duties designs with compensating controls, and a one-page awareness measurement plan with five behavioural metrics.
evaluationCriteria: Every risk category has an owner with the authority to change the exposure, and the justification says why
Compensating controls are specific enough to be implemented and auditable, not generic statements such as increased monitoring
Each awareness segment maps to named dangerous actions rather than generic awareness themes
Each metric has a threshold and an explicit board-level question it answers
No metric can be satisfied by an administrative action alone

items.title: CISM Domain 1 - Risk Management and the Security Risk Lifecycle
items.summary: How a security risk moves from identification through analysis and treatment to a defensible acceptance, and how the security risk register becomes the primary instrument of the risk conversation with the business.
objectives: Describe an end-to-end information security risk lifecycle with named entry and exit criteria
Distinguish inherent, residual and acceptable risk and connect each to a governance decision
Design a risk acceptance that is bounded, evidenced and owned by an accountable business executive
Operate a security risk register that is decision-grade rather than a document repository

sections.heading: The Risk Lifecycle in Security Terms
sections.body:
The security risk lifecycle is the discipline of moving a risk from an unexamined state to a managed state and keeping it there as conditions change. The stages are familiar from ISO 31000, but security-specific practice adds important detail to each one.

Identification is continuous, not annual. Sources include threat intelligence, vulnerability scanning, penetration test findings, incident retrospectives, third-party assessments, audit findings, regulatory notifications, employee reports, loss data, and the risk workshops. Most organisations over-rely on two of these and then wonder why their register does not reflect reality.

Analysis converts an identified issue into a position. For a technical vulnerability this means exploitation likelihood in your specific environment, business impact if exploited, and the effectiveness of existing controls. Analysis is where the biggest quality differences appear: two organisations facing the same CVE will assign different likelihood because one has no internet-facing instance and the other has forty thousand instances reachable from a flat network.

Evaluation asks whether the position is inside appetite and tolerance, and who is able to decide. Treatment sets the response. Monitoring watches for the conditions that would change the position. And critically, at each stage there must be a named owner and a date, because a risk without an owner is an unowned risk regardless of where in the lifecycle it sits.
bullets: Identification: continuous, multi-source - threat intel, scanning, testing, incidents, third parties, audits, loss data
Analysis: environment-specific likelihood and impact, not vendor severity scores
Evaluation: is the position within appetite, and who has authority to decide?
Treatment: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept or escalate, with a costed plan and owner
Monitoring: the conditions that would change the position, tracked as indicators

sections.heading: Inherent, Residual and Acceptable Risk
sections.body:
Three states of risk must be kept distinct in every register, report and conversation, because most security argument at the board fails because these are conflated.

Inherent risk is the exposure in the absence of controls - what would happen if every control that currently exists were removed. It is a property of the business activity and the environment, not of the organisation's maturity. Residual risk is the exposure that remains after the controls that are actually operating and effective have done their work. Acceptable risk is a governance conclusion: residual risk that sits inside the stated appetite and tolerance for that risk category and has been accepted by an authorised owner.

The operational implication is that residual risk must be based on evidence of control effectiveness, not on the existence of a control. An organisation that has a written procedure for privileged access review but has not run a review in eleven months has the inherent risk of privileged compromise, not a reduced one. This is the single most common error in security risk registers and it systematically understates exposure.

Reporting should present all three. A board that sees only residual scores believes the organisation is safer than it is. A board that sees only inherent scores believes nothing is being done. The instructive presentation shows inherent, the controls relied upon, the evidence of their effectiveness, the resulting residual, and the gap to appetite.
table: Exposure with no controls applied - a property of the activity and environment
Treated as the current position, which overstates the organisation's maturity
Exposure after controls that are operating and effective
Computed from documented controls rather than evidenced effectiveness
Residual risk within appetite, accepted by an authorised owner
Assumed by default because nobody objected at the time
sections.callout: If you cannot evidence that a control operated during the period you are reporting on, you have the inherent risk number, not the residual one. Say so in the report.

sections.heading: Risk Acceptance with Consequences
sections.body:
Risk acceptance is the mechanism by which an organisation stops pretending a risk is not real and starts managing it consciously. Done well it is a positive, bounded, documented act. Done badly it is a signature on a spreadsheet that nobody reads for two years.

A defensible acceptance has eight components. The risk statement in plain language, with the exposure quantified as far as it can be. The specific scenario or scenarios it covers. The controls that remain in place and the evidence they are working. The acceptance rationale - why the organisation prefers this exposure to the alternatives. The approver, named, with their role demonstrating authority for this risk category and this value. The expiry date, because most acceptances should be reviewed within a year and some much sooner. The consequence - what will actually happen if this materialises, stated plainly, because this is what converts an abstract acceptance into a genuine informed decision. And the review trigger, the event that forces the acceptance back to the committee before expiry.

The consequence field is what most organisations omit and it is the most valuable. When a risk owner writes that the consequence of accepting unauthenticated access to the customer portal would be regulatory penalty, reputational damage and notification of 400,000 data subjects, the approval becomes real. Without it, acceptance is a formality.

Separately, distinguish risk acceptance from risk deferral. Deferral - we will deal with it next quarter - is not acceptance, and it should be tracked in a different view with a different ageing measure. Any risk that has been deferred beyond a quarter with no treatment progress is an escalation candidate.
bullets: Eight components: statement, scenario, remaining controls, rationale, named approver, expiry, consequence, review trigger
State the consequence in plain numbers - who is affected, what is lost, what is notified
Acceptance is a governance act with a named authority, not a default outcome of silence
Track deferrals separately with ageing; anything overdue is an escalation candidate

sections.heading: Operating a Decision-Grade Risk Register
sections.body:
Most security risk registers are repositories that nobody uses to make decisions. The test of a decision-grade register is simple: can you walk into the governance committee and answer, from the register alone, what the organisation's top security exposures are, who owns each, what was decided about them, and when the decision expires?

A decision-grade register has seven attributes per entry. A unique identifier and title written in plain business language. The business context - what process, system or customer set is affected. The inherent and residual position with the analysis assumptions stated. The treatment, owner and due date. The linked controls with evidence references. The decision history, including who accepted what and when. And the next review date with the trigger that will bring it forward.

Two operational habits separate registers that work from registers that gather dust. First, link the register to treatment work: each accepted or mitigated risk points at a ticket, a project or a control test, so that the register and the programme cannot drift apart. Second, require the register to be the single source for the executive report - no parallel spreadsheets, no separate risk summaries - so that the number the board sees is the number the team manages.

Quality checks you should run quarterly: how many entries have not been reviewed in 90 days, how many have an expired acceptance with no re-decision, how many have a treatment owner who has left, and how many are duplicates of each other under different names. Deduplication is worth attention because register inflation creates the illusion of coverage while actually reducing clarity about what matters.
table: Connects the risk to an activity the business recognises
Makes the analysis auditable and challengeable
Converts a description into a commitment
Connects the register to what is actually operating
Prevents silent rollover of old acceptances

sections.heading: The CISO's Position in Enterprise Risk
sections.body:
Security risks do not exist in isolation from the enterprise risk universe. They sit inside a portfolio of operational, financial, regulatory, people and third-party risks, competing for the same capital and the same executive attention. A CISO who presents security risks in a separate register, reviewed in a separate meeting, with a separate appetite, ends up negotiating from a weak position and occasionally accepting risk that the enterprise risk view already excludes.

The constructive approach is to use a consistent taxonomy and scoring method across domains, so that a security exposure and an operational disruption can be compared honestly. Where that is not possible - and it often is not, because different functions own different methods - at least agree the interfaces: which risks are dependencies of which, which share a common cause, and which share a common treatment. A common cause analysis is especially valuable in cyber: a single identity provider compromise or a single cloud region failure will generate risks that appear in multiple registers, and only a portfolio view catches the correlated exposure.

Your seat at the enterprise risk table is earned by contribution, not title. What you bring that a generalist risk manager does not is a detailed understanding of how the technical estate produces or fails to produce the control, and a realistic view of what security treatment can achieve. Deliver that in the enterprise forum and you will be asked for input on non-security risk decisions that carry cyber consequences - a new payment channel, a cloud migration, an acquisition. That is where the CISO's influence is actually won.
bullets: Use a shared taxonomy and scoring method across domains wherever possible
Where methods differ, map dependencies and common causes explicitly
Correlated exposures appear in multiple registers and only a portfolio view finds them
Earn the enterprise table through the quality of contribution, not through title

examples.title: Unsigned acceptances across a healthcare group
examples.context: Your hospital group has 11 residual risks above tolerance. Nine of them were accepted by a department head in 2021 with no expiry and no stated consequence. The CISO has just been asked to present the register to the board risk committee and the CFO has asked whether the group could take insurance against them instead.
examples.outcome: A good outcome is a triage that separates the nine legacy acceptances from the two current ones: each legacy acceptance is reopened, re-quantified in light of the current threat picture, given a consequence statement and an expiry, and either re-accepted by an executive with authority or converted into a funded treatment. On insurance, the honest answer is that cyber insurance typically transfers financial loss and incident response costs but not the regulatory, contractual and reputational consequences, so the answer to the CFO is that insurance is a partial treatment layered on top of a managed position, not a substitute for one.

examples.title: Correlated risk across two registers
examples.context: In a telecom operator, the enterprise risk register carries an 'extended outage in core network' risk owned by network engineering, and the security register carries an 'unauthorised access to network management interfaces' risk owned by your team. Both are rated amber. The annual board report presents them in separate sections and the total exposure looks manageable.
examples.outcome: A good outcome surfaces the correlation in the portfolio view: the security exposure is one of the credible causes of the operational one. You bring this to the joint forum, propose treating the management-interface exposure as a driver of the operational risk, and the combined treatment (privileged access monitoring, out-of-band management, configuration assurance) is funded on the strength of the operational impact rather than the security score alone.

practicalExercise.title: Run a security risk lifecycle on a real scenario
practicalExercise.brief: You will take a realistic security exposure through the full lifecycle and produce the artefacts a governance committee would expect to see.
steps: Choose an exposure that is plausible for your organisation - for example credential stuffing against a customer portal, an unpatched internet-facing service, a third-party processor with production access, or an over-privileged service account.
Write the risk statement in plain business language, naming the affected asset, the business process and the potential consequence, and state the inherent risk position with your assumptions.

List the controls you would rely on to reduce exposure. For each, state how you would test whether it actually operated during the last 90 days, and note any control you cannot evidence - treat that as no control for scoring.
Compute the residual position and compare it to a stated appetite for that risk category. Decide the treatment, and name the owner, the cost band and the due date.

Draft a one-page risk acceptance memo containing all eight components, including a consequence statement in plain numbers, or draft a treatment proposal if you decided not to accept. Then write the three-sentence summary you would read aloud to the committee.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A lifecycle pack: risk statement, control effectiveness assessment, residual calculation, treatment decision with owner and date, and either an acceptance memo with all eight components or a treatment proposal.
evaluationCriteria: Residual risk is derived from evidenced control effectiveness, and any control that could not be evidenced is explicitly treated as absent
Assumptions behind likelihood and impact are stated and are specific to the actual environment
The treatment decision names an owner, a cost band and a date, and is consistent with the stated appetite
The acceptance memo contains all eight components, including a consequence statement expressed in plain numbers
The spoken summary is under two minutes and would satisfy a non-technical director without jargon

items.subtopic: Assessment methodology, threat intelligence and vulnerability governance
items.title: CISM Domain 2 - Information Risk Management
items.summary: How to run an information risk assessment that produces a defensible position, turn threat intelligence into decisions rather than feeds, and govern vulnerability management as a risk process rather than a patching treadmill.
objectives: Select and apply a risk assessment methodology appropriate to scope, regulatory context and available data
Distinguish qualitative, quantitative and hybrid assessment approaches and justify the choice
Convert threat intelligence into prioritised, owned decisions through an intelligence cycle
Govern vulnerability management as a risk treatment process with severity, context and evidence

sections.heading: What an Information Risk Assessment Is For
sections.body:
An information risk assessment answers three questions for a defined scope: what could go wrong, what would it cost if it did, and what should be done about it. Everything else in Domain 2 is a technique for answering those questions better. The scope is not a formality. An assessment of 'the organisation' is not an assessment; an assessment of the internet-facing retail banking estate supporting a 2.4 million customer base during the October to January peak is an assessment, and it produces findings that can be compared to appetite and funded.

Three failure modes are worth naming because they account for most poor assessments. The first is the technology inventory as the scope: scanning every server and calling it an assessment. That produces a vulnerability list, not a risk position. The second is treating the assessment as a point-in-time event with a report at the end. The third is the assessment that ends with a rating and no decision, so nothing changes and the next cycle starts from zero.

A modern assessment is also continuous in character. The assessment baseline can be refreshed continuously from detection data, control testing and third-party assessments, with a formal full assessment at a defined cadence. The governance question is not whether you re-scanned but whether any given risk position can be defended as current on the day it is asked about.
bullets: Scope must be stated as business context: services, customers, data, dependencies, and the period covered
An assessment that ends in a rating rather than a decision is not finished
Refresh continuously, assess formally at a defined cadence, and be able to date any stated position
Assessment output is a set of risk positions with owners, treatments and decisions requested

sections.heading: Methodologies: Qualitative, Quantitative and Hybrid
sections.body:
The methodological choice is a business decision with consequences, not a technical preference. Three approaches dominate practice.

Qualitative assessment uses ordered scales for likelihood and impact and produces a rating. It is fast, cheap, understandable by every audience, and the standard approach for most programmes. Its weakness is that the scale anchors differ between assessors, so a 'high likelihood' in a banking assessment and a 'high likelihood' in a telecom assessment may not mean the same thing, and it cannot support financial decisions.

Quantitative assessment estimates the range of possible loss with an explicit model, most commonly a factor or Monte Carlo approach on a loss distribution. It supports comparison against financial appetite, insurance and capital decisions. Its weakness is data demand and false precision: a modelled figure derived from a single incident will convey confidence it has not earned.

Hybrid approaches are the pragmatic norm in mature programmes. Quantify where the data supports it - typically the top exposures and the scenarios with loss history - and use qualitative assessment elsewhere, with the two calibrated against each other so the rating scale remains meaningful. The governance discipline is to document the calibration: when you say a risk is 'high' on the qualitative scale, what range of loss does that correspond to?

Whichever you choose, three practices separate professional assessment from amateur assessment. Document the assumptions - threat sources, control strengths, exposure - so the result can be challenged. Use the organisation's own evidence, not vendor severity scores, for exposure. And record what would change the assessment, so the next refresh is incremental rather than a restart.
table: Breadth of coverage, fast decisions, mixed audiences
Fast, cheap, explainable to a board
Scale anchoring drift, no financial comparability
Top exposures, insurance and capital decisions, large loss events
Data hungry, false precision if inputs are weak
Mature programmes with a mix of exposures
Requires discipline in maintaining the calibration bridge
sections.callout: Never let a vendor severity rating enter your register unadjusted. A CVSS 9.8 on an isolated, unexposed appliance and a CVSS 6.5 on an internet-facing authenticated gateway are very different business exposures.

sections.heading: The Intelligence Cycle: From Feed to Decision
sections.body:
Most organisations have far more threat intelligence than they use. They buy feeds, subscribe to bulletins, receive advisories and then experience a strange sense that none of it changed anything. The reason is that they treat intelligence as a product rather than as a cycle with a decision output.

The cycle has six stages. Requirements: what decisions do you actually need to be better at? Collection: what sources give you that? Processing: turning raw indicators into a usable form. Analysis: interpreting them in the context of your estate and business. Dissemination: getting the right thing to the right person at the right time. And feedback: did the intelligence change a decision, and if not, why not.

Requirements are the stage most organisations skip, and skipping it is why feeds go unread. The CISO's job is to articulate the handful of decisions intelligence improves: which vulnerabilities to treat first, whether a specific actor is likely to target this sector, whether a compensating control is needed for a specific business process, whether a new detection should be deployed, and whether the threat profile changes the assumptions in an existing assessment.

For each of those, define the requirement in terms of a latency target and a trigger. A good specification looks like this: when a new vulnerability with a vendor severity of 9 or above is confirmed to affect an internet-facing asset, produce a prioritised treatment instruction within 48 hours, with the environment-specific exploitation likelihood and an owner. That is intelligence with a contract. A generic advisory with a PDF attached is a commodity.

Context is what makes threat intelligence valuable and it is entirely internal. Knowing that a credential-stuffing campaign is targeting retail banking means little until you know which of your assets use the same credential store, whether your customer password policy supports the observed patterns, whether your multi-factor deployment covers the affected channel, and how your detections would show it. Build that asset and control context or the intelligence stays abstract.
bullets: Requirements first: name the decisions intelligence must improve and the latency target for each
Collection follows requirements - do not buy feeds because they are available
Processing and analysis depend on internal context: asset exposure, control estate, identity landscape
Dissemination is a design problem - who acts, within what time, with what instruction
Feedback: measure how many intelligence products resulted in a decision, and retire the ones that never do

sections.heading: Governing Vulnerability Management
sections.body:
Vulnerability management is the most mature, most metric-driven and most poorly governed security process in most organisations. The metrics exist - mean time to remediate, patch compliance percentage, number of criticals open - and they measure the wrong thing: closure speed, not risk reduction.

The governance shift is from severity-based prioritisation to risk-based prioritisation, and it requires three inputs. Exposure: is the asset reachable by an untrusted party, from where, and does it sit on a path to something valuable? Business criticality: what does this asset do for revenue, customers, safety or regulatory obligation? Threat activity: are there known actors actively exploiting this class of vulnerability, and does your threat intelligence say your sector is targeted?

Combine these into a prioritisation rule that the organisation can defend. For example: internet-facing, business-critical assets with a confirmed exploited vulnerability go into an emergency change window with a 24-hour target; internet-facing assets with exploited vulnerabilities go to 7 days; all internet-facing criticals to 30 days; internal crown jewels to 30 days; the remainder to the standard maintenance cycle. Publish the rule, and let business owners see it, because the rule is what determines whose work is interrupted.

Two supporting practices matter as much as the rule. First, a vulnerability exception process with named expiry, compensating controls and an owner - the same discipline as risk acceptance, because an unpatched critical with a compensating control is a treatment, not a gap. Second, evidence: the board should see the number of assets outside their remediation target, the total count by tier, the age of the oldest exception, and the coverage of the rule. Do not report a patch compliance percentage without also reporting the count of unpatched internet-facing crown jewels, because the percentage hides exactly the thing you care about.
table: Exposure plus business criticality plus active exploitation
Tiered targets by exposure and criticality, published
Named owner, compensating control, expiry, reviewed at committee
Counts and ageing by tier, plus coverage of the published rule
sections.callout: Speed of patching is a means. The governance question is whether the residual exposure is acceptable, and that requires knowing what is still exposed, not what percentage was closed.

sections.heading: Linking Assessment to Treatment Decisions
sections.body:
The value of an assessment is realised only when it produces decisions. Design your outputs so that every finding ends in one of four requests: accept with owner and expiry, treat with funded plan and date, defer with a stated condition and a short deadline, or escalate to the executive or board because it breaches appetite or exceeds the security function's authority.

That last category is the one organisations underuse. A sound assessment routinely finds exposures that no single business owner will accept, because the treatment is expensive and the benefit is shared. The correct response is escalation with a decision framework already prepared - options, costs, risks of each option, and a recommendation - not a warning that leaves the committee without a decision to make.

Two final disciplines close the loop. Traceability: every treatment should point back to the finding that generated it, so that a later audit can follow the chain from a stated risk to a control to evidence. And re-assessment: define in advance when a treatment is considered effective and how you will test it. A treatment that is never verified is an assumption, and assumptions accumulate quietly until the next incident.
bullets: Every finding ends in one of four requests: accept, treat, defer, escalate
Escalate with a decision pack - options, costs, risks and a recommendation - never a bare warning
Maintain traceability from finding to treatment to evidence
Define effectiveness criteria and verification method for each treatment at the point of approval

examples.title: Threat intelligence that changed a control decision
examples.context: A regional bank subscribes to a commercial threat feed. Six months after subscribing, the CISO asks what decisions the feed has improved and gets a list of advisories. Meanwhile, a physical intrusion at a branch last year led to a credential compromise. The bank's active directory holds a large number of accounts with service-desk-style passwords, and the feed has twice reported credential-stuffing campaigns against retail banking credentials.
examples.outcome: A good outcome reframes the requirement: the decisions the feed must improve are vulnerability and access prioritisation, credential policy, and detection coverage. The bank maps its feed alerts onto its own asset and identity context, discovers the exposed account population, and uses active-exploitation intelligence to justify a funded privileged and service-account password remediation ahead of the standard cycle. The feed's value is then measured in decisions changed, not advisories received.

examples.title: Replacing a patch compliance metric in a healthcare group
examples.context: Your group's IT function reports 96 per cent patch compliance to the board. The compliance figure is dominated by thousands of workstations. The CISO notes that the group's eleven public-facing services and its imaging systems have patch timelines of up to 180 days because they sit in a change freeze. A regulator has recently asked about the risk position on clinical system availability.
examples.outcome: A good outcome replaces the single percentage with a tiered model: exposure-based targets for internet-facing and clinical systems, a published prioritisation rule, an exception process with compensating controls such as enhanced monitoring and network segmentation for clinical systems, and a board metric reporting counts and ageing by tier. The narrative changes from a high compliance number that hides exposure to a specific statement about the residual position on clinical availability, which is what the regulator actually asked.

practicalExercise.title: Design an information risk assessment and a threat intelligence requirement
practicalExercise.brief: You will produce two artefacts: the scope, method and output specification for an information risk assessment, and a threat intelligence requirement specification that names the decisions it improves.
steps: Define the assessment scope as business context. State the services, customer sets, data classifications, third-party dependencies, geographies and time window covered, and list what is explicitly out of scope with a reason for each exclusion.
Choose a methodology - qualitative, quantitative or hybrid - and justify the choice in two sentences against the scope, the data you actually have, and the decisions the output must support.
Write the output specification: the fields each finding must contain, the decision each finding must request, the evidence sources you will use, and the cadence of refresh.

Write a threat intelligence requirement specification with three to four requirements. Each must name the decision improved, the trigger condition, the required latency, the format, and the internal context that must accompany it.

Design the vulnerability prioritisation rule for this organisation as a short table of tiers with exposure criteria, criticality criteria, exploitation criteria, target remediation windows, and the exception handling route.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A four-part pack: assessment scope and methodology, output specification, threat intelligence requirement specification, and a tiered vulnerability prioritisation rule.
evaluationCriteria: Scope is expressed in business terms with explicit exclusions and reasons
Methodology choice is justified against data availability and the decisions required, not chosen by habit
Each output specification field serves a downstream decision rather than a reporting need
Each intelligence requirement names a trigger, a latency and the internal context needed to act
The prioritisation rule is publishable to business owners and produces different treatment for different exposure profiles
